item.title: Large language models poorly capture how word order shapes representations of sentence meaning in the human brain.
item.description:
eLife
Large language models based on the transformer architecture are now capable of producing human-like language. But do they encode and process linguistic meaning in a human-like way? Here, we address this question by analysing 7T fMRI data from 30 participants reading 108 sentences each. These sentences are carefully designed to disentangle sentence structure from word meaning, thereby testing whether transformer representations of sentence meaning resemble those formed by the brain. Using representational similarity analysis, we compared representations from eight transformers and eleven other semantic models to brain activity in language regions of interest. We found that while transformer models match brain representations better than models that completely ignore word order, all transformers poorly match human brain representations of sentences that require sensitivity to structural relations such as semantic roles (who did what to whom). Further, transformers were significantly inferior to models explicitly designed to encode the structural relations between words. Our results provide insight into the nature of sentence representation in the brain, highlighting the critical role of sentence structure. They also cast doubt on the claim that transformers represent sentence meaning similarly to the human brain.

item.title: Mapping the topographic organization of the human zona incerta using diffusion MRI.
item.description:
eLife
The zona incerta (ZI) is a deep brain region originally described by Auguste Forel as an 'immensely confusing area about which nothing can be said'. Despite the elusive nature of this structure, mounting evidence supports the role of the ZI and surrounding regions across a diverse range of brain functions and as a candidate target for neuromodulatory therapies. Using in vivo diffusion magnetic resonance imaging and data-driven connectivity, we identify a topographic organization between the ZI and neocortex. Specifically, our methods identify a rostral-caudal gradient predominantly connecting the frontopolar and ventral prefrontal cortices with the rostral ZI, and the primary sensorimotor cortices with the caudal ZI. Moreover, we demonstrate how clustering and gradient approaches build complementary evidence including facilitating the mapping of a central region of the ZI, connected with the dorsal prefrontal cortex. These results were shown to be replicable across multiple datasets and at the individual subject level, building evidence for the important role of the ZI in mediating frontal lobe-associated tasks, ranging from motor to cognitive to emotional control. Finally, we consider the impact of this topographic organization on the refinement of neuromodulatory targets. These results pave the way for an increasingly detailed understanding of ZI substructures, and considerations for in vivo targeting of the ZI for neuromodulation.

item.title: Pediatric brain charts reveal ADHD biotypes with distinct developmental, molecular, and therapeutic profiles
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) exhibits profound clinical heterogeneity; however, its underlying neurobiological substrates remain unclear. Here, leveraging large – scale structural magnetic resonance imaging data from 12,663 typically developing children and 1,699 children with ADHD across Chinese and United States cohorts, we construct population specific pediatric brain charts via hierarchical Bayesian normative modeling to quantify individual deviations in cortical morphology. Data-driven clustering identifies two robust, cross – ethnically replicable ADHD biotypes: an infra – normal biotype characterized by widespread cortical thinning and a supra – normal biotype marked by cortical thickening. Multivariate analyses reveal distinct brain–behavior architectures: cortical deviations correlate preferentially with symptom severity in the infra–normal biotype but with both symptom severity and cognitive performance in the supranormal biotype. Clinically, the infra–normal biotype demonstrates a superior response to methylphenidate over atomoxetine, whereas the supra–normal biotype responds comparably to both. Transcriptomic analyses identify biotype–specific molecular signatures converging with ADHD genome–wide association study (GWAS) risk loci but exhibiting distinct expression patterns in the brain. These findings classify ADHD heterogeneity into neurobiologically distinct, clinically informed biotypes, providing a mechanistic framework for precision psychiatry in pediatric ADHD.

item.title: The Concise Language Paradigm in left and right hemisphere stroke: a longitudinal source-localized EEG study
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The mechanisms underlying language recovery after stroke remain poorly understood. Most previous studies have either focused on language comprehension or production and/or relied on hemodynamic measures, with limited complementary electrophysiological evidence. Here, we combined the Concise Language Paradigm (CLaP), assessing comprehension and production, with individualized electroencephalography (EEG) source reconstruction to investigate post-stroke language function and changes in hemispheric dominance over time. In two sessions, we tested stroke-free controls, individuals with left hemisphere (LH) or right hemisphere (RH) stroke. Participants with stroke were assessed two and seven months post-stroke. EEG data were analyzed using event-related potentials and time-frequency representations, followed by source reconstruction based on state-of-the-art individual MRI-derived forward models. Laterality indices were calculated to assess changes in hemispheric dominance between sessions. Behaviorally, the LH group showed low performance at two months followed by overall improvement, whereas the RH group mainly improved in functional communication. EEG activity was significantly modulated by task condition across comprehension and production contrasts. Source-level results in controls were consistent with established language-related networks, serving as regions of interest for the stroke analyses. In the stroke groups, hemispheric dominance differed between LH and RH stroke participants, with LH participants showing systematic shifts from left- to right-hemisphere dominance between sessions, if not already right-hemisphere dominant at two months. Our study provides evidence on comprehension and production performance after stroke using a single paradigm. These findings demonstrate dynamic changes in hemispheric dominance during post-stroke recovery, ultimately highlighting the value of individualized EEG source reconstruction to investigate post-stroke plasticity.

item.title: Unstable word form representations and greater reliance on right hemisphere during word learning in adults with a history of developmental language disorder
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Impairment in acquiring new vocabulary is a persistent deficit in developmental language disorder (DLD), but its cortical substrates remain unclear. We investigated learning of new words in young adults with DLD and typically developing (TD) control participants using magnetoencephalography (MEG). Participants were exposed to spoken real words and two sets of pseudowords, with shared beginnings, in two MEG sessions. One set of pseudowords was actively trained for three days, paired with fantasy animal pictures. Both groups learned new pseudowords, but adults with DLD recalled fewer items and confused similar sounding pseudowords more often than TD adults. MEG recordings revealed robust left temporal learning effects in both groups, along with left inferior frontal involvement. The DLD group additionally showed stronger right-hemispheric involvement and a significant right temporal learning effect for the newly learned words. Furthermore, only the DLD group showed changes in the left and right temporal responses for the real words after the learning phase, indicating altered lexical access for familiar words after integration of new word forms with overlapping phonology into the mental lexicon. Together, the findings suggest persisting problems in creating and accessing stable and distinctive phonological memory representations for word forms in adults with DLD, along with altered hemispheric balance in processing.

item.title: Functional and Structural Neuroanatomic Correlates of Intraoperative Anesthetic Dose-Adjusted EEG Alpha Power Among Older Surgical Patients
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Background: Alterations in intraoperative electroencephalography (EEG) alpha power and anesthetic dose-adjusted EEG alpha power (ADA-FP alpha power) have been associated with both preoperative cognitive impairment and postoperative delirium (POD) among older surgical patients, yet the neurologic underpinnings of alterations in these anesthetic brain response patterns are unknown. Methods: We conducted a single center prospective observational cohort study (ALADDIN), of older adults undergoing non-cardiac/non-cranial surgery, which included preoperative structural and resting state functional MRI, lumbar punctures to obtain CSF, 32 channel intraoperative EEG recordings, and repeated POD assessments. To account for anesthetic dose, frontoparietal EEG alpha power (ADA-FP alpha power) was adjusted using our established formula: [intraoperative alpha power]/(2.5 - end-tidal MAC fraction). Multivoxel pattern analysis (MVPA) with follow-up seed-to-voxel analyses identified functional connectivity patterns associated with intraoperative ADA-FP alpha power. Voxel-wise regression analysis with threshold free cluster estimation (TFCE) correction was used to evaluate associations between cortical thickness and ADA-FP alpha power. CSF biomarker values were obtained from NULISA proximity extension assays. Delirium incidence and severity was assessed with the 3-Minute Diagnostic Confusion Assessment Method (3D-CAM). Delirium severity area under the curve (AUC) during hospitalization was defined as the sum of all 3D-CAM delirium severity scores within the postoperative hospitalization period (for up to 7 days after surgery). The Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) was used in cases of non-verbal/intubated patients. Results: ALADDIN enrolled 215 patients, of whom 168 underwent surgery and had high-quality intraoperative EEG data (44.6% female; mean age 70.9 years). MVPA showed that ADA-FP alpha power was associated with altered functional connectivity within the bilateral frontal poles, left superior frontal gyrus and the right superior parietal lobule (p-FWE < 0.05). Seed-to-voxel analyses revealed that higher ADA-FP alpha power was associated with increased connectivity between DMN MVPA regions and DMN, DAN and salience/ventral attention and decreased connectivity with visual regions. Conversely, right superior parietal lobule connectivity shifted towards greater DMN segregation and increased somatosensory/motor coupling (p-FWE < 0.05). Lower ADA-FP alpha power was also associated with lower cortical thickness in left occipitotemporal and superior parietal cortices (TFCE-corrected p < 0.05). ADA-FP alpha power was also lower among participants with (vs those without) postoperative ward/floor delirium (mean difference, 1.33; 95% CI, 0.22 to 2.44; p=0.019), and ADA-FP alpha power was inversely associated with peak delirium severity (spearman's rho = -0.26; 95% CI, -0.40 to -0.11; p <0.001) and delirium severity AUC (spearman's rho = -0.28; 95% CI, -0.42 to -0.13; p < 0.001). Discussion: These findings suggest a functional and structural neuroanatomic basis for the decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power values seen among some older surgical patients, which may explain the association between decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power and increased rates of both preoperative cognitive impairment and postoperative delirium. More specifically, these findings suggest that altered default mode and dorsal attention network connectivity is linked to decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power and raise the possibility that preoperative/baseline functional connectivity alterations within these networks may play a role in delirium risk.

item.title: The joint modulation of language distance and task demands on the neural mechanisms underlying bilingual lexical processing
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Whether bilinguals share the same neural mechanisms for processing their first language (L1) and second language (L2) is a question of broad interest to researchers. Existing studies have accumulated substantial evidence, yet findings remain divergent. The primary sources of inconsistency lie in the language distance between bilinguals' L1 and L2, as well as differences in experimental tasks. Leveraging the advantages of meta-analysis, the present study examined brain activation patterns during L1 and L2 lexical processing in two groups of bilinguals: Chinese–English bilinguals with distant language distance (logographically–alphabetic) and alphabetic–alphabetic bilinguals with close language distance—across different tasks (phonological and semantic). Results showed that in phonological tasks, Chinese–English bilinguals recruited the left inferior parietal lobule/supramarginal gyrus more for L2, a region implicated in orthography-to-phonology conversion; in contrast, alphabetic bilinguals with close language distance shared overlapping neural mechanisms for L1 and L2. In semantic tasks, Chinese–English bilinguals engaged the left middle frontal gyrus and left precuneus more for L1 to support orthography-to-semantics conversion. In contrast, alphabetic bilinguals recruited the left middle temporal gyrus more for L1 for phonology-to-semantics conversion, and engaged language-control regions including the left middle frontal gyrus/inferior frontal gyrus, insula, and inferior parietal lobule more for L2. Further comparisons of brain activation during language-switching tasks between the two bilingual groups also revealed that alphabetic bilinguals with close language distance required greater involvement of executive control regions. Collectively, these findings indicate that the differential brain activation patterns observed when bilinguals process L1 and L2 arise from differences in underlying cognitive processes, jointly driven by language distance and task demands.

item.title: Neuroanatomy of Orthorexia Nervosa: Emerging Insights from Structural Neuroimaging
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Objective There are no published studies in the contemporary scientific literature that have directly applied neuroimaging techniques (such as fMRI, PET, or structural/functional MRI) to individuals with orthorexia nervosa (ON) to characterize brain alterations specific to this condition. Although interest in ON is increasing, a critical area of investigation concerns its phenomenological overlap with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and other feeding and eating disorders (FED). The present study aims to examine morphological brain differences in individuals with ON using high-resolution 3D T1-weighted MRI, with the goal of determining whether structural profiles observed in ON are comparable to those seen in OCD and in established eating disorder phenotypes. Methods Twenty-seven participants (12 females, 15 males) were enrolled in the study and underwent a comprehensive psychometric assessment including the ORTO-15, Italian-Düsseldorf Orthorexia Scale (I-DOS), Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS), and the Multidimensional Perfectionism Scale (MPS). Participants were stratified into those exhibiting orthorexic behaviour and those without (healthy control group, HC) according to ORTO-15 scores. The imaging protocol included the acquisition of high-resolution three-dimensional T1-weighted MRI scans. Groups were compared regarding cortical and subcortical parameters in order to identify neuroanatomical differences associated with orthorexic behaviour. Results Morphometric analysis revealed a significant correlation between ORTO-15 score and cortical thickness (CT) in key brain regions. Specifically, lower ORTO-15 scores—indicative of greater orthorexic tendencies—were associated with a marked reduction in CT of the entorhinal cortex (EC). Conversely, an increased CT was observed in the right posterior cingulate cortex (PCC). Discussions The observed alterations in the EC and PCC suggest that ON may share neurobiological patterns with OCD and FED. These findings support the notion of ON as a distinct yet transdiagnostic clinical entity. However, the small sample size highlights the need for further large-scale investigations to confirm the presence and reliability of these potential neurobiological biomarkers.

item.title: Changes in gray matter volume associated with gait speed and muscle mass in older adults with mild cognitive impairment.
item.description:
Journal of Alzheimer's disease : JAD
BackgroundMild cognitive impairment (MCI) is an early stage of cognitive decline between normal aging and dementia. Gait speed, a key marker of physical function, has been associated with both cognitive decline and brain atrophy. Sarcopenia, characterized by age-related loss of muscle mass and function, has also been linked to structural brain changes.ObjectiveTo investigate the associations between sarcopenia, its individual components and regional gray matter volume (GMV) in older adults with MCI.MethodsThis cross-sectional study included 234 older adults with MCI. Sarcopenia, gait speed, handgrip strength, and appendicular skeletal muscle mass index (ASMI) were assessed according to the 2019 Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia criteria. Brain T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging was analyzed using voxel-based morphometry. Voxel-wise group comparisons were performed to identify GMV differences after adjustment age, sex, comorbidity, depressive symptoms, nutritional status, and total intracranial volume.ResultsSlower gait speed was significantly associated with lower GMV in the bilateral putamen and left superior frontal cortex. Lower ASMI was associated with higher GMV in the left inferior temporal cortex. No significant GMV differences were found by sarcopenia status or handgrip strength.ConclusionsSlower gait speed is associated with reduced GMV in motor-related brain regions, indicating early brain structural changes in older adults with MCI. Although lower ASMI was associated with higher GMV, this finding should be interpreted cautiously. These findings highlight the complex interactions between physical function and brain structure, emphasizing gait speed as a potential indicator of brain health in older adults with MCI.

item.title: The uncinate fasciculus in frontotemporal dementia subtypes: A systematic review and meta-analysis of diffusion-tensor imaging studies.
item.description:
Journal of Alzheimer's disease : JAD
BackgroundFrontotemporal dementia (FTD) is a leading cause of early-onset neurodegeneration with selective frontal and temporal lobe degeneration. Despite well-characterized gray and white matter atrophy patterns across FTD subtypes, the extent of degeneration of the uncinate fasciculus (UF) tract has not been systematically quantified across FTD subtypes.ObjectiveTo compare uncinate fasciculus fractional anisotropy, mean diffusivity, radial diffusivity, and axial diffusivity between frontotemporal dementia subtypes and healthy controls.MethodsWe systematically searched PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science and performed a random-effects meta-analysis of diffusion tensor imaging studies published between 2011 and October 2025 according to PRISMA 2020 guidelines.ResultsWe systematically reviewed 11 studies and performed a meta-analysis of 540 participants across 10 studies. We found that all FTD subtypes demonstrated significant degeneration of the UF compared to controls. The greatest effect sizes were observed when comparing the left UF between the semantic variant primary progressive aphasia (svPPA) and controls (FA: SMD = -2.5396, 95% CI: -3.7914, -1.2878, p < 0.0001; RD: SMD = 2.2414, 95% CI:1.7972, 2.6855, p < 0.0001; AD: SMD = 1.9831, 95% CI: 1.1434, 2.8227, p < 0.0001; MD: SMD = 2.5268, 95% CI: 1.9993, 3.0542, p < 0.0001), while the behavioral variant (bvFTD) showed the largest reduction in right UF fractional anisotropy. Within-group analyses revealed significant left-right asymmetry in svPPA and non-fluent aphasia (nfvPPA), with greater left UF involvement, while bvFTD and controls showed no hemispheric differences.ConclusionsWe highlight the UF as a promising tract for understanding disease mechanisms and developing imaging biomarkers in FTD.

item.title: An exploratory synthetic MRI-derived FLAIR-DIR contrast in olfactory-limbic regions in mild cognitive impairment.
item.description:
Journal of Alzheimer's disease : JAD
BackgroundOdor identification impairment is an early feature of Alzheimer's disease and predicts memory decline, but its microstructural basis remains unclear.ObjectiveTo evaluate FD, a semi-quantitative synthetic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived Fluid-Attenuated Inversion Recovery (FLAIR)-Double Inversion Recovery (DIR) contrast, against myelin volume fraction (MVF) in olfactory-limbic brain regions of patients diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment (MCI).MethodsSixteen healthy controls (HC) and 17 individuals diagnosed with MCI completed olfactory and cognitive testing and underwent 3T MRI using a QALAS sequence. MVF maps were generated and FD was computed as (FLAIR - DIR)/FLAIR. Group differences were examined in olfactory-limbic gray matter and associated white-matter tracts, and voxel-wise regression assessed FD-odor identification associations, including models adjusted for voxel-wise MVF. Region of interest and voxel-wise analyses were exploratory and largely uncorrected for multiple comparisons.ResultsCompared with HC, MCI showed lower FD across olfactory-limbic gray matter and white-matter pathways, including hippocampus, amygdala, orbitofrontal cortex, thalamus and corpus callosum, whereas MVF differences were more limited. Better odor identification was associated with higher FD in hippocampal/parahippocampal regions and insula, persisting after MVF adjustment. MVF showed positive associations in the right parahippocampal gyrus, left thalamus and genu of the corpus callosum. In an exploratory secondary analysis reported in the Supplemental Material, FD-based classification exceeded chance but was not separable from age alone.ConclusionsFD is a semi-quantitative relaxation-contrast metric showing regional patterns partially distinct from MVF. These exploratory findings require replication in larger, demographically matched, biomarker-confirmed cohorts before FD can be regarded as a marker of early olfactory-limbic microstructural change in MCI.

item.title: Temporal lobe cortical thickness and cognition in paediatric cancer survivors previously treated with chemotherapy.
item.description:
British journal of haematology
Long-term neurocognitive outcomes in paediatric cancer survivors treated with chemotherapy remain incompletely characterized, particularly in relation to cortical structure. Prior neuroimaging studies have included limited representation of racial and ethnic minority survivors. We analysed temporal lobe cortical thickness and cognition in paediatric cancer survivors treated with chemotherapy (n = 21; 8-25 years post-chemotherapy; aged 15-34 years) and age-matched controls (n = 21). Cognition was assessed using National Institute of Health (NIH) Toolbox scores. Cortical thickness of nine bilateral temporal regions was derived from T1-weighted 3T magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) using FreeSurfer. Group differences and brain-cognition associations were analysed using adjusted regression models with false discovery rate correction. Survivors scored lower on crystallized (p < 0.001), fluid (p = 0.013) and total cognition scores (p = 0.001). They showed reduced temporal lobe cortical thickness (2.62 ± 0.13 vs. 2.74 ± 0.11 mm; p = 0.001), with reductions in seven subregions. Greater thickness was associated with better cognitive performance in 10 of 27 associations, most prominently for crystallized cognition. Fully corrected T-score sensitivity analyses showed crystallized cognition remained lower in survivors (p = 0.044). Paediatric cancer survivors previously treated with chemotherapy showed reduced temporal lobe cortical thickness, which was associated with worse crystallized cognition, suggesting a potential structure-function association.

item.title: Action features dominate cortical representation during natural vision.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Cortical resources are allocated into systems specialized for processing ecologically relevant features of the world. These features are typically studied in isolation using controlled experimental stimuli, making it difficult to assess the relative importance of different kinds of features that tend to overlap during natural vision. In the current study, we evaluated the relative contributions of action, agent, and scene features in predicting cortical activity while participants viewed a 1-h nature documentary. We tested four sets of model features: semantic vectors capturing the observed action, agent, and scene features derived from an annotation of the stimulus, as well as low-level visual motion-energy features. We used banded ridge regression to fit vertex-wise encoding models from the combination of all four sets of features. While each set of features predicted neural activity in the expected areas, the action features predicted more widespread activity. A variance partitioning analysis revealed that the action features captured the most unique variance in neural activity across a much larger extent of cortex than the agent or scene features. Our findings suggest that cortical activity during dynamic, natural vision is dominated by features for understanding the actions of others.

item.title: Multimodal associations between posterior hippocampus glutamate metabolism, visual cortex connectivity, and intrusive trauma reexperiencing symptoms.
item.description:
Molecular psychiatry
Hippocampal dysfunction is implicated in posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), particularly intrusive reexperiencing symptoms, and may be mediated by glutamatergic excitotoxicity. Markers of glutamate dysfunction (higher glutamate to N-acetyl aspartate levels; Glu/NAA) in the hippocampus (HPC) have been linked to reexperiencing symptoms. However, the HPC demonstrates heterogeneity along its anterior-posterior axis, with different functional connectivity patterns and PTSD symptom associations, motivating investigations into glutamate metabolism in anterior and posterior HPC subregions (a/pHPC). To this end, 121 symptomatic trauma-exposed adults with current trauma reexperiencing symptoms completed magnetic resonance spectroscopy and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging to examine the regional specificity of HPC Glu/NAA associations with reexperiencing symptoms and the link to a/pHPC functional connectivity. PTSD symptoms were assessed with the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale for DSM-5. Reexperiencing symptom severity was associated with greater Glu/NAA in the pHPC, but not aHPC. pHPC Glu/NAA was further linked to stronger functional connectivity between the pHPC and visual cortex (VC), which in turn correlated with more severe reexperiencing symptoms. This strengthened pHPC-VC connectivity explained the shared variance between pHPC Glu/NAA and reexperiencing severity, suggesting dysregulated glutamate metabolism in the pHPC may contribute to reexperiencing symptoms through functional connectivity with the VC. These findings replicate prior work linking HPC Glu/NAA to trauma reexperiencing symptoms and provide novel evidence of this association in the pHPC, but not aHPC, which is mediated by its functional connectivity with the VC. This multimodal investigation supports translational models of glutamatergic dysfunction in trauma-related disorders and highlights new targets for pharmacological and neuromodulatory interventions.

item.title: Distinct profiles of white matter diffusivity in obesity and bipolar disorders: An ENIGMA bipolar disorders study in 2166 individuals.
item.description:
Psychological medicine
Background Bipolar disorders (BD) are associated with a wide range of brain white matter abnormalities, but results vary across studies. This heterogeneity likely relates to effects of additional clinical/diagnostic variables, including medications and obesity, on white matter in BD. In this mega-analysis, we studied the links between relevant clinical variables and four diffusivity measures. Methods We obtained diffusion tensor imaging-derived fractional anisotropy (FA), mean, axial, and radial diffusivity (MD, AD, RD) values from 910 individuals with BD and 1256 healthy controls across 16 research sites in the ENIGMA-BD Working Group. We used principal component analysis to detect patterns of covariance across white matter tracts and studied associations between multivariate patterns of white matter alterations and demographic and clinical variables, including body mass index (BMI), medications, and diagnostic information, using mixed regression models. Results Higher BMI was associated with lower PC1 FA and higher PC1 RD; BD was associated with higher PC1 MD, while treatment with antiepileptic medications was associated with lower PC1 FA, higher PC1 MD, and PC1 RD. Conclusions We found FA and MD are weakly associated, providing complementary information, and there are unique associations between specific diffusivity measures and clinical predictors. Treatment with antiepileptics may inflate the statistical effects of BD on white matter. By using all diffusivity measures and accounting for additional clinical factors, we can gain new insights into brain correlates of severe mental illness.

item.title: Decoding individual differences in mental information from human brain responses predicted by deep neural networks.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Brain decoding using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has high potential for evaluating unobservable mental information that varies across individuals in everyday situations. Although estimating individual differences in mental information using brain decoding could be effective for social applications, especially in neuromarketing, the physical constraints and high costs of fMRI limit the practical application in real-world settings. To overcome these limitations, we propose a framework to estimate individual differences in decodable mental information using brain responses predicted by deep neural networks (DNNs). In this framework, DNN-based models are trained to predict fMRI responses to natural movie scenes. Then, additional fMRI measurements are no longer required because mental information for new movie scenes can be decoded from the predicted responses instead of the measured ones. A large-scale analysis revealed that the proposed predicted-response decoding captures individual difference patterns consistent with those derived from conventional measured-response decoding across various cognitive domains. Of the 88 cognitive labels associated with movie scenes, individual difference patterns could be captured for more than 70% of the labels. This framework offers a promising approach for evaluating personal mental information with substantially reduced reliance on fMRI, thereby expanding the potential for social applications of brain decoding.

item.title: Digital Twin Control Framework Uncovers Individualized Cross-Scale Links Between Functional Connectivity Deviations, Communication Impairment, and Molecular Mechanisms in Autism.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Background Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is hallmarked by pronounced inter-individual heterogeneity in brain function and clinical manifestations. Conventional neuroimaging studies yield highly inconsistent findings, as extrinsic confounding factors and intrinsic disease heterogeneity mask ASD-specific functional connectivity (FC) signatures, hampering the identification of individualized neural mechanisms linked to symptom severity. Methods We developed a digital twin control analytical framework based on deep contrastive learning. By comparing each ASD participant with their matched digital twin control, we quantified individual-specific FC deviations. Principal component analysis was applied to extract the core aberrant pattern, followed by multi-dimensional analyses and validation including clinical correlation, transcriptomic decoding, neurotransmitter and mitochondrial co-localization, as well as disease and cognitive enrichment. Results The model effectively disentangled disease‑related from non‑disease‑related variations. The identified dominant aberrant FC pattern was significantly associated with Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS) communication scores, suggesting its associated with to communication impairment. This pattern showed convergent associations with synaptic pathways, excitatory/inhibitory neuronal signatures, critical developmental windows and subcortical structures, and exhibited negative spatial association with multiple neurotransmitter systems and mitochondrial respiratory complexes. Biological validation further supported its ASD specificity and communication‑related cognitive relevance. Conclusions Leveraging the twin control analytical framework, this study provides an exploratory cross-scale framework linking individualized FC deviations with clinical, transcriptomic, neurochemical, and mitochondrial maps. The findings indicate that communication difficulties in ASD may partly arise from multi-scale disturbances in neural integration, social-perceptual processing and activity-dependent cellular energy regulation.

item.title: Coarse motor-state structure across paired preoperative fMRI and intraoperative ECoG in patients with brain tumors.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Presurgical motor mapping in patients with tumors near eloquent motor cortex is commonly based on task-evoked activation maps, yet local BOLD responses may be difficult to interpret in lesion-affected tissue because of anatomical distortion, altered vascular coupling, and variability in task performance. In this study, we used a four-state motor paradigm spanning Action, kinesthetic motor imagery (IMG), Watch, and recent-action recall (REC) - to test whether coarse task-state relationships are preserved across paired preoperative fMRI and intraoperative ECoG in10 patients with brain tumors. Activation summaries and preoperative task familiarization were used to support task engagement, representational similarity analysis (RSA) was used to characterize within-modality state geometry, and cross-modal RSA was used to assess shared organization. Across modalities, Action and IMG showed relatively similar response patterns, Watch was more distinct, and REC occupied an intermediate position that should be interpreted cautiously because of the fixed task order. Cross-modal RSA showed positive correspondence between fMRI and ECoG representational dissimilarity matrices, supporting a shared coarse state structure rather than fine-grained equivalence between modalities. These findings support a hypothesis-generating, relation-based complementary framework for interpreting functional organization in patients with brain tumors, while the limited state space, clinically determined ECoG coverage, fixed task order, and indirect verification of internally generated states warrant cautious interpretation.

item.title: The Visual Cortex and Beyond: Investigating Long-Term Cortical Plasticity Following Monocular Deprivation.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Aim To characterise short- and long-term plastic changes in cortical and subcortical structures induced by ultra-long (five-day) monocular deprivation (MD), and to assess the extent and regional specificity of structural changes and their reversibility following the restoration of binocular vision. Methods In this single-arm longitudinal study, 21 healthy adults underwent five structural MRI sessions: at baseline, during MD on days 1, 3 and 5, and after a seven-day recovery period (day 12). MD was induced by occluding the right eye with a translucent eye patch for five consecutive days. Grey matter volume (GMV) changes were analysed using voxel-based morphometry (VBM) for whole-brain effects and generalised estimating equations (GEE) to model temporal trajectories in predefined cortical and subcortical regions. Results Ultra-long MD induced dynamic GMV changes in primary and higher visual cortices, with exploratory changes also in subcortical and cerebellar structures. VBM showed cumulative volume increases in bilateral occipital cortex, including calcarine, lateral occipital and fusiform regions, and adjacent cerebellar lobules, peaking between days 3 and 5. Region-wise modelling resolved the temporal build-up of these changes across visual, subcortical and sensorimotor regions; after correction for multiple comparisons, a time-dependent effect remained in occipital and ventral occipito-temporal cortex (occipital pole, fusiform and calcarine cortex), converging with the voxel-wise result. Following binocular restoration, an exploratory GMV decrease was observed selectively in the left middle occipital gyrus, while an exploratory increase was observed in the left hippocampus, compatible with persistent plasticity in associative memory networks. Conclusion Prolonged sensory imbalance via ultra-long MD induces rapid, region-specific and possibly persistent GMV plasticity in the adult brain. These changes follow temporally stratified trajectories across visual, subcortical and integrative systems, consistent with models of homeostatic and hierarchical plasticity. Corrected evidence supports cumulative occipital plasticity during deprivation; whether the exploratory extra-visual and post-recovery changes reflect persistent adaptation requires confirmation. MD-based paradigms thus offer a controlled window on structural plasticity in both healthy individuals and clinical populations.

item.title: Translational evidence for habenula's role in human addiction: A scoping review.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Addiction is characterized by persistent substance use or engagement in behaviors despite adverse consequences and impaired control, but its expression varies substantially across individuals, substances, and severity. Within one influential neurocircuitry framework, addiction processes are organized into binge, withdrawal, and preoccupation stages. Preclinical research implicates the habenula across these processes but indicates that its contribution varies across drugs, subdivisions, and experimental models. Research on the human habenula in addiction remains fragmented, and the extent to which it converges with preclinical mechanisms is unclear. This scoping review synthesized evidence on the human habenula in addiction and examined its convergence with preclinical findings. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, databases and grey literature were searched in November 2025, with literature surveillance continued through April 2026. Human studies reported reduced fronto-habenula white-matter integrity, elevated habenula-striatal resting-state functional connectivity, withdrawal-related habenula-frontal connectivity, increased habenula blood flow during opioid withdrawal, altered task-evoked responses to reward and feedback, and nicotine-related genetic signals. By contrast, morphological studies found no consistent differences in habenula structure across addiction samples. Most human neuroimaging studies could not distinguish the medial and lateral habenula, limiting direct comparison with subdivision-specific preclinical mechanisms. Overall, across human and preclinical studies, the evidence does not support a unitary habenular alteration across addiction. Cross-species convergence was strongest for withdrawal-related activity, particularly for opioids, and for nicotine-related molecular mechanisms, but remained limited by differences in substances, circuits, measures, and paradigms. Future studies using subdivision-sensitive imaging and more comparable cross-species designs are needed.

item.title: Insular subregional dysfunction in panic disorder: A multimodal MRI study.
item.description:
Journal of affective disorders
Background The spatial organization of insular abnormalities across connectional-architecture-defined subregions in panic disorder (PD) remains unclear. We examined structural and resting-state functional measures using the Brainnetome Atlas. Methods Forty-nine medication-naïve patients with PD and Fifty healthy controls underwent structural and resting-state MRI. Gray matter volume (GMV), amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation (ALFF), and regional homogeneity (ReHo) were assessed across six insular subregions. Four prespecified functional connections were examined, together with exploratory Granger causality analysis between dIg and S1 and an AAL3 whole-insula comparison. Results dIg-S1 functional connectivity was reduced in PD (β = -0.148, 95% CI [-0.248, -0.048], pFDR = 0.017). ALFF showed a Group × Subregion interaction (F(5,578) = 4.162, p = 0.001). Only the ventral agranular insula (vIa) showed significantly higher ALFF after false discovery rate (FDR) correction (pFDR = 0.016), with a larger group effect than other subregions. The interaction persisted after temporal signal-to-noise ratio (tSNR) adjustment (F(5,577) = 2.582, p = 0.025), but the vIa-specific effect was nonsignificant in a separate vIa-only tSNR-adjusted model (p = 0.194). ReHo was directionally lower across all six subregions, but no contrast survived FDR correction. No robust subregional GMV differences or significant group differences in exploratory Granger causality were detected. Adjusted AAL3 whole-insula differences were nonsignificant. Conclusions PD showed measure-dependent insular functional alterations, including reduced dIg-S1 coupling and vIa-predominant ALFF differences, with the latter sensitive to signal quality and spatial smoothing.

item.title: Infant Negative Affect During Mother-Infant Interaction Is Associated with Neonatal Limbic-Prefrontal Connectivity in the First Month of Life.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry. Cognitive neuroscience and neuroimaging
Background Early caregiving may shape neonatal limbic circuit organization, yet whether microanalytically coded interaction quality relates to neonatal limbic-prefrontal connectivity is unknown. We tested associations between infant and maternal affect during mother-infant interaction and neonatal limbic-prefrontal cortex (PFC) connectivity. Methods At approximately 30 days postnatal, 143 mother-infant dyads from the Healthy MiNDS cohort (São Paulo, Brazil) completed a video-recorded interaction coded with the Coding Interactive Behavior (CIB) system; infant negative affect was the percentage of interaction time in distress. Neonates underwent resting-state fMRI; limbic-PFC connectivity was quantified by principal component analysis of amygdala and hippocampus seed-to-ROI maps. Covariate-adjusted regressions tested associations. Results Infant negative affect was associated with right amygdala-PFC (β = -0.247, p = .003) and right hippocampus-PFC connectivity (β = -0.202, p = .021), both surviving FDR correction and robust across multiple analytic approaches. The amygdala association was limited to infant distress-related behaviors, whereas maternal positive expressiveness showed an independent, opposing association (β = 0.202, p = .019); no other CIB measure was significant. Exploratorily, connectivity was associated with sleep problems at 18-24 months in females (r = -.324, p = .030). Conclusions The emotional quality of early caregiving is associated with neonatal limbic circuit organization: infant distress is selectively associated with weaker amygdala-PFC connectivity, whereas maternal positive affect shows an independent opposing association. These findings identify the mother-infant relationship as a modifiable input to neonatal brain development.

item.title: Positive-affective and negative-cognitive brain-behavior axes in clinical high risk for psychosis.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Background Individuals at clinical high risk for psychosis (CHR) present with heterogeneous combinations of positive, negative, and affective symptoms, cognitive difficulties, and functional impairment. However, reproducible multivariate links between this multidomain phenotype and brain morphology remain limited. This study explored the multivariate brain-behavior associations in CHR using a data-driven approach. Methods Baseline data from 720 CHR participants from the Accelerating Medicines Partnership® Schizophrenia program (AMP® SCZ) were analyzed using sparse canonical correlation analysis to identify associations between 95 regional brain volumes and 28 behavioral variables indexing symptoms, cognition, and functioning. Generalizability was tested using leave-one-network-out cross-validation (PRoNET and PRESCIENT), and stability was assessed using bootstrapping and leave-one-site-out analyses. Associations with demographic, clinical and site-related variables were examined. Results Two brain-behavior dimensions generalized across networks. A positive-affective axis (r=0.21-0.23), linking higher depression, anxiety/stress, positive symptoms and anhedonia with predominantly frontal-cingulate-insular volume reductions and relatively larger corpus callosum and putamen volumes. This axis was associated with comorbid depression, cannabis use and family history of depression or affective psychosis. A negative-cognitive axis (r=0.17-0.18) linked greater asociality, alogia, emotional withdrawal, blunted affect, and motor retardation, poorer cognition and functioning with reduced cerebellar and parietal volumes, and relatively larger lateral ventricles and corpus callosum. This axis was associated with lower IQ and poorer premorbid adjustment. Conclusions Two partially dissociable brain-behavior dimensions were identified: a positive-affective axis capturing the co-expression of affective and attenuated positive symptoms, and a negative-cognitive axis suggestive of neurodevelopmental vulnerability.

item.title: The Spectrum within the Spectrum: Neural Heterogeneity in Autism.
item.description:
Behavioural brain research
Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) encompasses diverse behavioral, cognitive, and neural profiles that vary widely across individuals. Because diagnosis remains predominantly behavior-based, clinically meaningful within-spectrum differences are often missed. Recent advances in neuroimaging analysis have created opportunities for the identification of distinct neural profiles within ASD. These new avenues provide ways to examine intra-ASD heterogeneity directly, identifying person-specific brain-behavior patterns that group-level comparisons fail to capture. The present systematic review focused on neuroimaging methods (i.e., resting-state fMRI; rs-fMRI, cortical morphology) that emphasized heterogeneity-informed outcomes based on normative modeling, data-driven subtyping, clustering analysis and similar analytic choices. For rs-fMRI, findings showed that differences in connectivity within the default mode and salience networks were linked to social-communication and language impairments, with subtype-specific patterns emerging across samples. In cortical thickness and surface area, studies identified distinct developmental trajectories and individual deviation profiles, with prefrontal and temporal regions often tied to repetitive behaviors and social-communication difficulties. Voxel-based analyses revealed subgroup-specific gray matter alterations, including cerebellar and cortical differences, that aligned with variation in repetitive behaviors and social difficulties. Collectively, this emerging evidence supports the notion that neural heterogeneity in autism is a core feature rather than a limitation. Embracing individual variability can provide crucial insight into the inconsistencies and contradictions of earlier case-control and group-level findings. Moving forward, autism research must prioritize heterogeneity-based methods to establish reproducible subtypes and individualized brain-behavior links.

item.title: Individual Differences in Sustained Attention Tune Semantic Abstraction in Neural Encoding of Narratives
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Neural encoding modeling for narrative comprehension -- using LLM embeddings to predict the temporal dynamics of neural activation -- is widely used to evaluate how well the brain represents certain semantic information. This approach, however, typically collapses semantic representation into a scalar fidelity score aggregated across participants, overlooking potentially rich individual differences and qualitative differences in naturalistic neural representations. In the current study, we addressed this gap by investigating how neural semantic encoding varies across individuals with sustained attention, and whether this difference is qualitative in addition to quantitative. Using fMRI data from 49 participants listening to an audiobook, Le Petit Prince, in English, we trained encoding models with GPT-2 embeddings at varying layers and forecasting lengths. Encoding models trained on high-level embeddings (from the 8th layer of GPT-2) showed significant brain-LLM alignment in 73 of 122 cortical and subcortical ROIs, concentrated in the temporal cortex and the default mode network. Functional connectivity strength in a validated connectome-based predictive model of sustained attention correlated with encoding performance in 18 ROIs, most strongly in the insula and in control and attention networks, with no ROI showing significant opposite relationship. Decomposing semantic information by levels of abstraction showed that the neural signature of sustained attention was selectively associated with a greater proportion of high-level gist information encoded in the frontoparietal and attention networks, while the opposite relationship emerged for proportion of low-level information. Sustained attention scores further predicted stronger predictive coding of upcoming narrative content across multiple networks across the whole brain (control, default mode, salience/ventral attention, limbic, and somatomotor networks). These findings suggest that sustained attention does not uniformly amplify neural semantic encoding, but instead shifts neural representations toward more compressed, gist-level formats that support anticipation of upcoming content. Individual differences in brain-LLM alignment can be a signature of representational strategy rather than noise, with potential utility for cognitive phenotyping.

item.title: Development of Neonatal Functional Brain Network Organisation and Its Association with Childhood Neurodevelopmental Outcomes
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The human brain undergoes rapid dynamic changes in the neonatal period that are essential for later cognitive and behavioural performance. Using resting-state fMRI data from 394 neonates (325 term-born, 69 preterm-born) within the first month after birth, we characterised the early development of functional network organisation, the effects of preterm birth, and the association between neonatal functional organisation and later neurodevelopmental outcomes in infancy (18 months) and childhood (4-6 years). We found increased functional integration and segregation across a wide range of functional sub-networks and increased mean functional connectivity strength (mean FCS) within the subcortical and cerebellar regions with increasing PMA at scan. Compared with term-born neonates, preterm-born neonates showed significantly lower mean FCS, functional integration and segregation globally. We further showed that whilst neonatal functional brain network organisation was not associated with neurodevelopmental outcomes measured during infancy (18 months), it was associated with later neurodevelopmental outcomes in early childhood (4-6 years). Specifically, higher functional integration and segregation at birth were linked with lower SDQ total difficulties score at 4-6 years. Our findings suggest that neonatal functional brain organisation reflects not only transient developmental processes, but also stable individual differences that provide insight into neurodevelopmental outcomes in later childhood.

item.title: Faster peak alpha frequency precedes higher menstrual pain in adolescence
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Brain differences in chronic pain are almost always measured after years of pain experience, leaving unresolved whether they create vulnerability to pain or result from it. Uniquely, menstrual pain has a developmentally scheduled onset (menarche, the first menstrual period), allowing the brain to be characterized before and after pain exposure occurs. Here we used longitudinal 64-channel EEG to measure resting brain activity in adolescents once before (n=250) and twice after (n=161, n=140) menarche. Before their first period, adolescents who later reported higher menstrual pain (30 or greater on a 0 to 100 VAS) already showed faster occipital peak alpha frequency compared to those who reported lower menstrual pain, a difference that persisted in the early (3 to 14 months) post-menarche time period. In contrast, oscillatory power and functional connectivity did not differ by menstrual pain group, suggesting that the widespread functional brain alterations reported in adults with painful periods take years to emerge. Peak alpha frequency increased, and theta power and connectivity decreased across the menarchal transition, consistent with typical adolescent maturation. However, longitudinal analyses stratified by higher and lower menstrual pain group suggested group specific timings for these neurodevelopmental changes. Overall, these findings suggest that early menstrual pain is not associated with widespread alterations in neural oscillations, but aspects of menstrual pain susceptibility may be reflected in resting peak alpha frequency. To our knowledge, this is the first neurophysiological trait shown to precede the onset of menstrual pain.

item.title: A brain-behavior generative model links individual brain dynamics to perceptual decisions
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Perceptual decision speed varies across individuals and trials. Explaining this variability requires linking individual brain anatomy, neural dynamics, and behavior, yet whole-brain models typically reproduce brain signals without behavior, whereas behavioral models lack anatomical constraints. Here we introduce a brain-behavior generative model in which whole-brain dynamics on each participant's structural connectome generate both single-trial electroencephalography (EEG) and reaction times. Fitted to 17 participants performing motion discrimination, the models reproduced individual event-related potentials and reaction-time distributions. Joint fitting enabled the models to predict whether held-out trials were relatively fast or slow within each stimulus condition. In silico silencing further predicted where, how, and when each person's brain controls decision speed. Sensorimotor regions affected decision speed consistently across most participants, whereas the same parietal region had opposite effects in different participants. These opposite effects reflected whether the region acted mainly through network dynamics or the decision readout. Temporal analyses suggested that early activity largely set decision speed, whereas late EEG mainly tracked the unfolding decision. These results show that brain-behavior generative modeling can link individual brain dynamics to perceptual decisions and yield testable predictions of why decision speed varies across individuals and trials.

item.title: Field Position and Subjective Number of Headers Are Associated with Subcortical Volumes in Female Soccer Players.
item.description:
AJNR. American journal of neuroradiology
Background and purpose Repetitive head impacts (RHI) from soccer headers could be linked to neurodegeneration, but their effects on young, active athletes are still under debate. This exploratory, cross-sectional study aimed to generate hypotheses about the relationship between soccer headers, brain volume alterations, and neuropsychological function in female soccer players. The analysis focused on brain regions previously identified as vulnerable to RHI. Materials and methods Nineteen semiprofessional female soccer players (mean age: 22.4 ± 4.1 years) and 15 noncontact-sport controls underwent structural MRI. Players were assessed for neuropsychological function and measures of exposure (field position, subjective number of headers, age at first exposure, and total years played). Subcortical gray and corpus callosum white matter volumes were calculated using FreeSurfer for all participants. Group differences in brain volumes were assessed. Among players, associations between brain volumes, exposure measures, and neuropsychological function were analyzed, controlling for multiple comparisons using a 25% false discovery rate. Results This study found no statistically significant group differences in brain regional volumes. Among players, a higher subjective number of headers correlated with lower left thalamic (r = -0.54; P = .02) and posterior corpus callosum volumes (r = -0.57; P = .01), whereas field positions with an expected higher number of headers were linked to lower volumes of the right nucleus accumbens (r = 0.58; P = .01) and hippocampus (r = 0.72; P = .001). No statistically significant associations were found for other exposure measures, brain volumes, or any of the neuropsychological outcomes. Conclusions A higher subjective number of headers among female soccer players was associated with group-level findings regarding reduced subcortical gray and central white matter brain volumes in our small sample of female soccer players. Although these findings are exploratory, group level, and of uncertain clinical significance, they provide hypotheses for future studies and suggest directions for further investigation.

item.title: Neural correlates of infant dialect discrimination: An fNIRS study.
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
The present study investigated the neural correlates of infant discrimination of very similar linguistic varieties (Quebecois and Parisian French) using functional Near InfraRed Spectroscopy. In line with previous behavioral and electrophysiological data, there was no evidence that 3-month-olds discriminated the two regional accents, whereas 5-month-olds did, with the locus of discrimination in left anterior perisylvian regions. These neuroimaging results suggest that a developing language network relying crucially on left perisylvian cortices sustains infants’ discrimination of similar linguistic varieties within this early period of infancy.

item.title: Frequency-Specific Cognitive Control Network Hypoconnectivity in Adolescents With Elevated Externalizing Symptoms
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background Externalizing symptoms during adolescence are associated with behavioral difficulties and an increased risk of adverse developmental outcomes, and are often accompanied by difficulties in self-regulation across cognitive and emotional domains. Although prior neuroimaging studies have reported altered brain connectivity in externalizing psychopathology, most evidence comes from functional magnetic resonance imaging, leaving frequency-specific electrophysiological network dynamics poorly understood. We examined resting-state electroencephalographic (EEG) functional connectivity in a community-based sample of 35 adolescents aged 13–15 years with relatively high or low parent-reported externalizing symptoms. Source-level connectivity was estimated using exact low-resolution electromagnetic tomography and lagged phase synchronization across delta-to-gamma frequency bands within the cognitive control network (CCN) and default mode network (DMN). Results Adolescents with higher externalizing symptoms showed reduced connectivity in five beta1- and gamma-band CCN connections, whereas no significant group differences were observed within the DMN. After adjustment for internalizing symptoms, bilateral anterior-insula connectivity in the beta1 band and left anterior insula–right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex connectivity in the gamma band remained significant. Lower left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex–right inferior frontal junction beta1 connectivity was also associated with greater self-reported physical aggression. Conclusions Elevated externalizing symptoms during adolescence may be linked to altered functional coordination within the cognitive control network. These findings highlight the potential value of frequency-resolved EEG connectivity for characterizing the neural correlates of adolescent externalizing symptoms.

item.title: Aperiodic EEG activity is a domain-specific marker of attentional aging in neurotypical adults.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Aperiodic neural activity has been reliably shown to be reduced among older adults, and these reductions are associated with age-related cognitive decline. These results suggest that aperiodic activity, as measured by the spectral exponent, might be a viable electrophysiological biomarker for cognitive aging. However, this has not been tested longitudinally, within participants, during normal aging. Here, we used a longitudinal cohort of either sex to test whether changes in aperiodic activity between two sessions, approximately 5 years apart, track behavioral change across two domains: sustained attention (Psychomotor Vigilance Test) and executive function (modified Simon task). We found that aperiodic activity declined within individuals after the interval, independent of age at baseline. This within-person change tracked concurrent changes in reaction times during sustained attention but was not associated with changes in any Simon task measure. Within a resampling framework, the aperiodic-PVT association was stable across cohort resamples and independently fitted partitions, though it was not confirmed in a small, frozen held-out set. These findings suggest the longitudinal decline in aperiodic activity tracks attentional processing speed rather than executive function, supporting its potential as a domain-specific biomarker of attentional aging in neurotypical populations.Significance Statement Aperiodic (non-oscillatory) neural activity, indexed by the aperiodic exponent, is known to decline in older adults, but whether this happens within individuals over just a few years, and in step with cognitive change, remains unclear. Here we leveraged scalp EEG and cognitive-behavioral data from 276 neurotypical adults, tested twice approximately five years apart, and found that the aperiodic exponent declines within individuals over this interval, independent of age at baseline. This decline tracked concurrent slowing on a sustained attention task, but not change on an executive function task, and only in EEG recorded before, not after, cognitive testing. Based on this dissociation, we propose that aperiodic exponent decline indexes attentional processing speed rather than general cognitive decline in neurotypical aging.

item.title: Probing the neural geometry of conscious object perception in time.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Conscious object recognition is a critical brain function, key to making sense of the plethora of visual inputs and guiding adaptive behavior. Yet, the sequence of neural processing underlying conscious object recognition remains unclear. Existing proposals alternatively suggest that conscious object recognition proceeds in a "coarse-to-fine" sequence or a "fine-to-coarse" sequence. Here, we recorded high-density EEG while participants of both sexes performed a threshold-level object recognition task under different viewing conditions. Both superordinate and basic-level category information emerged early in neural activity, followed by a late superordinate category representation in an abstract format that is disentangled from low-level object features. Strikingly, in the early period, while basic-level category information positively correlated with perceptual awareness, superordinate category information negatively predicted perceptual awareness. By contrast, both superordinate and basic-level category information positively correlated with objective categorization accuracy in the early period. In the late period, both levels of category information positively correlated with awareness. These results suggest that neural processing underlying conscious object perception proceeds from the basic to the superordinate category level.Significance statement Despite significant interests, the sequence of neural processing underlying conscious perception remains unclear. Here, we investigated the unfolding of neural events in time that support perceptual awareness of visual objects. Using a threshold-level object perception task involving three image conditions (normal, low-pass filtered, masked) and high-density EEG, we reveal that basic and superordinate category information both emerge early in the neural activity (at ∼100 ms), but only the basic-level category representation positively contributes to awareness. By contrast, the early superordinate category representation negatively correlates with perceptual awareness. At ∼300 ms, an abstract superordinate category representation emerges, which also positively correlates with perceptual awareness. Therefore, category-level neural processing underlying conscious object perception proceeds from the basic to the superordinate level.

item.title: A cortical semantic map integrates fractions and integers in the human brain.
item.description:
PLoS biology
How does the human brain represent the meaning of abstract symbols? Some theories postulate the existence of semantic spaces where concepts occupy positions that reflect their conceptual relationships. In the number domain, psychological evidence suggests that integers are represented along a mental number line which, with education, integrates higher-level number concepts such as fractions. To test this hypothesis, we recorded whole-brain 7T fMRI responses to integer and fraction symbols during an active magnitude comparison task designed to engage magnitude processing. Consistent with predictions, we found both behavioral and neural numerical distance effects. Activation vectors in intraparietal, inferior temporal, prefrontal, hippocampal, and parahippocampal cortices formed a two-dimensional semantic space organized by numerical magnitude and domain (fractions versus integers). Gaussian fits revealed a topographic map of numerical preferences in the anterior inferior parietal cortex, common to both domains. Our results suggest that, when educated adults engage in an explicit magnitude comparison task, their brain can construct an ordered representation that integrates fractions and integers, with a topographic organization in the anterior IPS/IPL.

item.title: DTI-Associated Blood Biomarkers in a Human Perioperative Brain Perturbation Model.
item.description:
Journal of neurotrauma
Circulating biomarkers of brain perturbation are rarely evaluated against anatomically localized in vivo imaging measures, limiting biological interpretation. We tested whether perioperative changes in candidate biomarkers were associated with diffusion tensor imaging (DTI)-defined microstructural changes in a controlled human perioperative model. In a paired cohort of 75 patients undergoing left-sided encephaloduroarteriosynangiosis, we obtained matched pre- and postoperative DTI and blood samples. Six biomarkers (ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase-L1 [UCH-L1], glial fibrillary acidic protein [GFAP], S100 calcium-binding protein B [S100B], neurofilament light chain, neuron-specific enolase, and protein tau) were quantified. Analyses included paired comparisons, region-of-interest-based cross-modal correlations, sparse canonical correlation analysis (sCCA) with bootstrap stability assessment, and patient-grouped regularized logistic regression for state discrimination. DTI showed perioperative changes in bilateral temporal-limbic regions and connected white matter, with the largest effects in left hippocampal and amygdalar territories on the operated side. UCH-L1, GFAP, and S100B showed the clearest paired increases and dominated internal perioperative-state discrimination. Blood-DTI associations were heterogeneous across biomarkers and states, and paired-change associations were not confined to these three markers. An observed three-biomarker panel discriminated perioperative state with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.914 in the test set. Several circulating biomarkers covaried with regional DTI measures in this exploratory perioperative cohort. UCH-L1, GFAP, and S100B were the most perioperatively responsive and state-discriminative markers, but the DTI-association pattern was not specific to this trio. The findings support a structure-associated framework for evaluating blood biomarkers against regional imaging changes; they do not validate these biomarkers for traumatic brain injury, and relevance to traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains hypothesis-generating.

item.title: Longitudinal Changes in Brain Connectivity and Structure after MRgFUS VIM Thalamotomy for Essential Tremor.
item.description:
Stereotactic and functional neurosurgery
Essential Tremor (ET) is the most common movement disorder. Magnetic Resonance-guided Focused Ultrasound (MRgFUS), an incisionless surgery involving thermal ablation of targeted brain regions, like the Ventral Intermediate Nucleus of the Thalamus (VIM) and surrounding white matter tracts, is an effective treatment option. Fractional Anisotropy (FA), a metric of diffusion tensor imaging, can be used to determine white matter structural integrity and their changes following MRgFUS. This study investigates white matter and morphological brain remodeling after MRgFUS VIM thalamotomy and its association with tremor improvement, assessed by the Clinical Rating Scale for Tremor (CRST), over the first postoperative year. We retrospectively analyzed 56 ET patients who underwent unilateral MRgFUS VIM thalamotomy. Subjects' CRST scores, T1-weighted MRI scans, and diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) scans were acquired pre-operatively and at three and twelve months post-operatively. FA maps were generated and registered to a standard space. Voxel clusters that exhibited significant change in FA over time were identified using FSL's cluster tool (p<0.001) and their change in FA value over time was Spearman correlated with relative change in CRST score. Deformation-Based Morphometry of T1-weighted images evaluated changes in structural volume, and a linear mixed-effects model was applied. We permuted these values 1000 times randomly to isolate significant (p<0.01) clusters related to the interaction between time and outcome and Spearman correlated them with relative improvement in CRST. Four main FA clusters demonstrated strong associations between CRST score and time. The insula produced consistent positive correlations at three (R=0.32, p=0.04) and twelve months (R=0.29, p=0.11). Yet, the visual cortex exhibited no significant association at three months (R=0.11, p=0.46), but did at twelve months (R=0.35, p=0.05), suggesting malleable white matter remodeling. Our morphometry analysis revealed two primary clusters located in the pre-supplementary motor area (pre-SMA) and visual cortex. The pre-SMA exhibited the strongest correlations at three months (three months: R=0.34, p=0.03, twelve months: R=0.17, p=0.36), while the visual cortex displayed a similar strength throughout (three months: R=0.20, p=0.18, twelve months: R=-0.22, p=0.23). These findings suggest that MRgFUS VIM thalamotomy is associated with broad structural tract and volumetric changes that extend beyond motor networks. Both analyses demonstrated post-treatment volume growth and increased tract structure in visual and cognitive regions. Correlation with tremor improvement indicates many of these changes may contribute to individual outcomes during the first post-operative year.

item.title: Infra-slow brain-heart-gut electrophysiological interactions reveal a co-ordinated multisystem physiological network in humans.
item.description:
The Journal of physiology
Growing evidence indicates that brain continuously interacts with other physiological systems through neural and non-neural pathways. The brain-heart and brain-gut axes play a central role in homoeostasis, allostasis and behaviour, but also in cognitive aspects, including emotion and decision-making. Disruptions in these axes have been linked to a wide range of cardiovascular, neurological and psychiatric disorders. Despite this evidence, triadic crosstalk between the brain, heart and gut remains largely unexplored. Brain activity, cardiac autonomic fluctuations and gastric rhythms all exhibit slow temporal components in resting state, suggesting that brain-heart-gut electrophysiological interactions may occur over time scales from the infra-slow (0.01-0.1 Hz) physiological range. Using open-access electrophysiological recordings from 28 healthy subjects at rest, we extracted time-varying power dynamics describing the activity of the three organs: brain alpha power, cardiac sympathetic and parasympathetic indices, and the power of the gastric rhythm. Statistical associations among these organs were quantified using the maximal information coefficient across the extended temporal delay range. Physiological interactions were confirmed using surrogate-based testing, which allowed us to construct the network topology of interactions between the three organs. Our findings show that triadic brain-heart-gut interactions form a multidirectional network primarily at infra-slow time scales during resting state. This study offers one of the first insights into the physiology of brain-heart-gut interplay, providing a methodological baseline for the development of more comprehensive biomarkers based on network dynamics capable of linking pathological conditions to dysregulation across multiple organ systems. KEY POINTS: First in-human, non-invasive investigation of parallel brain-heart-gut electrophysiological interactions in awake, healthy subjects. We analysed simultaneous electroencephalographic (EEG), electrocardiographic (ECG) and electrogastrographic (EGG) recordings and quantified strength and temporal scale of the derived time series associations to construct a large-scale network of interactions. We found that brain-heart-gut interactions extend into the infra-slow range (0.01-0.1 Hz), indicating that spontaneous fluctuations in the electrophysiological activity of one organ at rest are typically followed by corresponding changes in the other two. We consistently found a robust brain-heart-gut network topology across subjects, with multidirectional interactions and bodily dynamics converging towards midline central-posterior EEG regions. These findings provide one of the first endeavours in characterizing the physiology of brain-heart-gut interactions and a methodology with strong biomarker development potential.
